newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - World praises Blair's energy but real tests ahead.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - World praises Blair's energy but real tests ahead.

text.p: If there is one thing that impresses world leaders, it is a huge election victory.
The landslide which swept Tony Blair's Labour party to power on May 1, ending 18 years of Conservative rule, won open admiration from fellow heads of government whatever their political leanings.

Blair's honeymoon period at home has been matched abroad. His drive and charm won plaudits from foreign colleagues used to -- and often exasperated by -- John Major's efforts to calm feuds in his Conservative party by demonstrating "little England" truculence abroad.
"All the indications in the first 100 days are positive," said one Western diplomat in London who was reluctant to be named. "There is a level of energy that was not there before."
But energy can fade and honeymoons turn into fond memories in the face of the realities of life, and politics.

With Britain due to host a Commonwealth heads of government meeting in October, to assume the European Union presidency in January and to hold the summit of the Group of Seven plus Russia in May, tough times at the diplomatic top table lie ahead.
"The eyes are really going to be on Blair to see what leadership we can expect," said the diplomat, summarising the outlook of London-based diplomats for the year ahead.
HECTIC FOREIGN AGENDA
Blair began his term with a blitz of foreign travel.

A meeting in May with U.S. President Bill Clinton -- a political and personal soulmate -- dispelled the chill which had crept into the "special relationship" between Britain and the United States after the Conservatives' ill-judged and ineffective election help for Clinton's rival, George Bush, in 1992.

In Amsterdam for his first EU summit in June, Blair claimed a triumph for preserving control of Britain's borders while parading a new, constructive approach to Europe after years of Conservative doggedness and obstructionism.

A few days later, at the British leader's first G7 summit, Blair enlisted Clinton's support for the drive for peace in Northern Ireland and claimed a success for his "new Labour" campaign for flexible labour markets.

Apart from a minor hiccup when Italy bristled at remarks by Foreign Secretary Robin Cook that Britain wanted to be one of the three leading players in Europe alongside France and Germany, Blair and his government has not put a foot wrong.
Germany praised Blair's EU summit performance, with one Bonn source saying he had operated with "classic British efficiency" while presenting himself as a "committed European".

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl warmly welcomed Blair when he visited Germany last month, but had to put on a brave face as the new Labour leader lectured him about the need for economic reform across Europe and flexible labour markets.

But with Kohl's tax reform plans facing a blockade by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), which controls the upper house of parliament, any catalytic effect Blair may have had on German politics has been forgotten.

Blair's influence is being felt most in Germany in the ranks of the SPD, where Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder -- a top candidate to challenge Kohl in elections next year -- has increasingly been adopting "new Labour" views.
Schroeder's call for the SPD to ape Labour's efforts to widen its appeal beyond its traditional working class base have been dismissed as populism and criticised by left-wingers.

Denmark and Sweden, both wary of excessive European integration, have also found common cause with Blair's insistence that the EU should look at the long term and the needs of ordinary citizens rather than concentrate its efforts on making the European single currency work.
In France, the new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, who came to power a month after Blair, has also claimed kinship, citing a high priority for education and job creation.
NOT ALL ENTENTE CORDIALE
But commentators have detected strains -- fiercely denied by Blair and his aides -- between Jospin and the British premier.

Unlike Blair, Jospin is broadly opposed to the privatisation of state companies and defends a more robust brand of socialism than "New Labour", calling for a shorter working week and job creation in contrast to Blair's emphasis on flexibility. Both men believe in the value of a minimum wage.

Blair's recipe also worries France's Conservative President, Jacques Chirac, who does not want Jospin to ape the Labour leader's free-market policies. "I don't want (Jospin) to seek inspiration from Tony Blair's example...," Chirac said.
"France couldn't go as far in what we call liberalisation, flexibility, in some senses the questioning of guarantees and social rights," Chirac said in a July 14 National Day interview.
"Tony Blair is a very liberal man. I watch him and listen to him at all international talks. He's a very, very liberal man. Maybe he's right, but it's Britain, not France."
WARMER WELCOME FROM WASHINGTON
Far warmer are the signals from Washington, where Blair's cooperation on NATO enlargement and Bosnia, and his drive to breathe life into Northern Irish peace talks have been welcomed.
U.S. officials talk of "re-energised" links. "It's clear that in this 100-day period they are (cooperating), and in some cases with a little more energy and fervor than before," said one.
